title: Your Browser Now Has an AI Inside It: What to Know Before Turning It On
summary: AI browsers can now read your tabs and click buttons for you. One security flaw - prompt injection - cannot be fully patched. Here is what that means for you.
before: AI browser assistants work like secure, sandboxed tools that cannot be tricked by malicious websites.
after: Hidden text on any webpage can hijack the AI agent acting on your behalf. No vendor has a complete fix.
body:
For thirty years, browsers did one job: fetch a page and draw it on your screen. You did the rest. In 2026, that assumption is breaking. A new category of browser ships with an AI agent living inside it - one that can read what you are looking at, summarize it, and increasingly take actions on your behalf.

This is not hype. It is happening now, and it comes with a security trade-off that every user should understand before flipping the switch.

## The New Lineup

The AI browser category matured rapidly through 2026. The major players, as of 2026-09-27, include:

- **Perplexity Comet**: A standalone browser built around research and citations. Launched in July 2025 as a $200-a-month product, Perplexity dropped the paywall and now offers it free across iOS, Android, Windows, and Mac, with agentic 'Background Assistant' tasks reserved for paid tiers.
- **Gemini in Chrome**: Google's integration that added a virtual assistant for online tasks, with fuller autonomous browsing behind a paid tier
- **Edge Copilot**: Microsoft's built-in AI features
- **Brave Leo**: A privacy-first option that routes requests anonymously and offers on-device processing
- **Claude in Chrome**: An extension from Anthropic that lets Claude read, click, type, and fill in forms in your own browser using your existing logins. After piloting in 2025 and a beta for paid plans, Anthropic made it generally available on every paid Claude plan (Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise) on August 26, 2026. It lists roughly 15 million users on the Chrome Web Store as of September 2026, and remains Chrome-only on desktop.

OpenAI's ChatGPT Atlas browser, launched in October 2025, was the most aggressive early entry - but it no longer exists as a standalone product. OpenAI announced in July 2026 that it would fold Atlas into ChatGPT and Codex, and the standalone browser stopped working on August 9, 2026. Its browser-based agentic capabilities moved into an upgraded browser mode in the ChatGPT desktop app and a ChatGPT Chrome extension. The pattern is clear: AI features are increasingly moving into existing browsers rather than requiring you to switch.

## What These Agents Can Actually Do

An AI browser pairs a normal rendering engine with an agent that can read your pages and take multi-step actions for you. In agent mode, the browser views webpages and uses clicks and keystrokes "just as you would," letting it work across routine workflows using the same context and data a person would have.

They shine at reading, summarizing, and cross-tab research. The more autonomous options can fill forms, navigate between sites, and complete tasks you would normally do manually. The catch is that to be useful, the agent typically needs access to your logged-in sessions, email, and accounts.

## The One Risk That Cannot Be Patched

Here is the uncomfortable truth: **prompt injection** is a structural problem that may never be fully solved.

Prompt injection works because AI models cannot reliably distinguish between instructions and data. Every input - whether it comes from you, a document, a webpage, or an email - gets processed through the same mechanism. An attacker embeds malicious instructions in content the agent reads, and the agent treats those instructions as authoritative, overriding your actual intent.

OWASP, the nonprofit that tracks application security risks, ranked prompt injection as the number one LLM vulnerability again in its 2026 Top 10 for LLM Applications, published in early August 2026 - the third year running that it has topped the list. Notably, the 2026 edition was the first to weigh real-world incident data (drawn from thousands of reported incidents) alongside the practitioner vote, and prompt injection held the top spot even though relatively few successful attacks show up in public databases - a gap OWASP attributes to how hard teams work to contain it.

This is not a bug that a patch will fix. It is a property of how transformer-based models work: they process instructions and untrusted content within the same context, so prompting and filtering may reduce successful attacks but cannot reliably prevent a malicious input from influencing the model. When security researchers demonstrated that a few carefully placed words inside a shared document could steer how a browser agent behaved, they were not exploiting sloppy code - they were exploiting a fundamental design characteristic. Anthropic, for its part, says its own testing shows a sharp drop in successful attacks against Claude in Chrome, but still calls the chance of an attack "non-zero."

## Why This Matters More Now

The stakes rose in 2026 because these agents gained the ability to act. A chatbot that gives you a bad answer is annoying. An agent that clicks a button or sends an email on your behalf based on hidden instructions is a different category of problem.

The security industry's framing has shifted to match. OWASP's 2026 guidance urges builders to stop trying to make a model that cannot be fooled and instead design the surrounding system so that when the model is fooled, nothing important breaks - treating the job as containment and blast-radius control rather than perfect prevention.

## Practical Safety Rules

You do not need to avoid AI browsers entirely. But you should treat them as powerful tools with real limits:

- **No autonomous payments**: Never let an AI agent complete purchases or transfers without explicit confirmation from you
- **Require confirmation on consequential actions**: Any action that sends data, deletes something, or changes settings should pause for your approval
- **Use a limited browser profile**: Run agentic browsing in a profile that is not logged into your primary email, bank, or sensitive accounts
- **Keep sensitive tabs closed**: Do not leave important logged-in sessions open in the same window where an agent is browsing the open web
- **Watch for unexpected behavior**: If the agent does something you did not ask for, stop and investigate before continuing

The vendors are not hiding this risk. Anthropic's own guidance tells users to skip banking and health records, warns that some sites hide instructions that override yours, and advises pausing and reviewing if Claude acts unexpectedly - noting its classifiers are a defense, not a guarantee. But the fundamental problem remains: the agent cannot always tell the difference between your instructions and a malicious one hidden on a page.

## The Bottom Line

AI browsers represent a genuine shift in how we interact with the web. They are useful, improving quickly, and increasingly free. But the security model is not settled - and, as the Atlas shutdown in August 2026 showed, even the products themselves can change form fast. Until the security picture settles - if it ever does - treat these tools as assistants that need supervision, not autonomous agents you can fully trust with your logged-in life.
